Ah, distinctly I remember it was in the bleak December,
And each separate dying ember wrought its ghost upon the floor.
Eagerly I wished the morrow;--vainly I had sought to borrow
From my books surcease of sorrow--sorrow for the lost Lenore--
For the rare and radiant maiden whom the angels name Lenore--
                                   Nameless here for evermore.

And the silken sad uncertain rustling of each purple curtain
Thrilled me--filled me with fantastic terrors never felt before;
So that now, to still the beating of my heart, I stood repeating
"'Tis some visiter entreating entrance at my chamber door--
Some late visiter entreating entrance at my chamber door;
                                   This it is and nothing more."

Presently my soul grew stronger; hesitating then no longer,
"Sir," said I, "or Madam, truly your forgiveness I implore;
But the fact is I was napping, and so gently you came rapping,
And so faintly you came tapping, tapping at my chamber door,
That I scarce was sure I heard you"--here I opened wide the door--
                                   Darkness there and nothing more.

Deep into that darkness peering, long I stood there wondering, fearing,
Doubting, dreaming dreams no mortals ever dared to dream before;
But the silence was unbroken, and the stillness gave no token,
And the only word there spoken was the whispered word, "Lenore?"
This I whispered, and an echo murmured back the word, "Lenore!"--
                                   Merely this and nothing more.

Back into the chamber turning, all my soul within me burning,
Soon again I heard a tapping something louder than before.
"Surely," said I, "surely that is something at my window lattice;
Let me see, then, what thereat is and this mystery explore--
Let my heart be still a moment and this mystery explore;--
                                   'Tis the wind and nothing more.

Open here I flung the shutter, when, with many a flirt and flutter,
In there stepped a stately Raven of the saintly days of yore.
Not the least obeisance made he; not a minute stopped or stayed he,
But, with mien of lord or lady, perched above my chamber door--
Perched upon a bust of Pallas just above my chamber door--
                                   Perched, and sat, and nothing more.

Then the ebony bird beguiling my sad fancy into smiling,
By the grave and stern decorum of the countenance it wore,
"Though thy crest be shorn and shaven, thou," I said, "art sure no craven,
Ghastly grim and ancient Raven wandering from the Nightly shore--
Tell me what thy lordly name is on the Night's Plutonian shore!"
                                   Quoth the Raven, "Nevermore."

Much I marvelled this ungainly fowl to hear discourse so plainly,
Though its answer little meaning--little relevancy bore;
For we cannot help agreeing that no living human being
Ever yet was blessed with seeing bird above his chamber door--
Bird or beast upon the sculptured bust above his chamber door,
                                   With such name as "Nevermore."

But the Raven, sitting lonely on that placid bust, spoke only
That one word, as if its soul in that one word he did outpour
Nothing farther then he uttered; not a feather then he fluttered--
Till I scarcely more than muttered: "Other friends have flown before--
On the morrow _he_ will leave me, as my Hopes have flown before."
                                   Then the bird said "Nevermore."

Startled at the stillness broken by reply so aptly spoken,
"Doubtless," said I, "what it utters is its only stock and store,
Caught from some unhappy master whom unmerciful Disaster
Followed fast and followed faster till his songs one burden bore--
Till the dirges of his Hope that melancholy burden bore
                                   Of 'Never--nevermore.'"

But the Raven still beguiling all my sad soul into smiling,
Straight I wheeled a cushioned seat in front of bird and bust and door;
Then, upon the velvet sinking, I betook myself to linking
Fancy unto fancy, thinking what this ominous bird of yore--
What this grim, ungainly, ghastly, gaunt, and ominous bird of yore
                                   Meant in croaking "Nevermore."

This I sat engaged in guessing, but no syllable expressing
To the fowl whose fiery eyes now burned into my bosom's core;
This and more I sat divining, with my head at ease reclining
On the cushion's velvet lining that the lamp-light gloated o'er,
But whose velvet violet lining with the lamp-light gloating o'er
                                   _She_ shall press, ah, nevermore!

Then, methought, the air grew denser, perfumed from an unseen censer
Swung by Seraphim whose foot-falls tinkled on the tufted floor.
"Wretch," I cried, "thy God hath lent thee--by these angels he hath sent thee
Respite--respite and nepenthe from thy memories of Lenore!
Quaff, oh quaff this kind nepenthe and forget this lost Lenore!"
                                   Quoth the Raven, "Nevermore."

"Prophet!" said I, "thing of evil!--prophet still, if bird or devil!--
Whether Tempter sent, or whether tempest tossed thee here ashore,
Desolate, yet all undaunted, on this desert land enchanted--
On this home by Horror haunted--tell me truly, I implore--
Is there--_is_ there balm in Gilead?--tell me--tell me, I implore!"
                                   Quoth the Raven, "Nevermore."

"Prophet!" said I, "thing of evil!--prophet still, if bird or devil!
By that Heaven that bends above us--by that God we both adore--
Tell this soul with sorrow laden if, within the distant Aidenn,
It shall clasp a sainted maiden whom the angels name Lenore--
Clasp a rare and radiant maiden whom the angels name Lenore."
                                   Quoth the Raven, "Nevermore."

"Be that our sign of parting, bird or fiend!" I shrieked, upstarting--
"Get thee back into the tempest and the Night's Plutonian shore!
Leave no black plume as a token of that lie thy soul has spoken!
Leave my loneliness unbroken!--quit the bust above my door!
Take thy beak from out my heart, and take thy form from off my door!"
                                   Quoth the Raven, "Nevermore."

And the Raven, never flitting, still is sitting, still is sitting
On the pallid bust of Pallas just above my chamber door;
And his eyes have all the seeming of a demon's that is dreaming
And the lamp-light o'er him streaming throws his shadows on the floor;
And my soul from out that shadow that lies floating on the floor
                                   Shall be lifted--nevermore!

poems.title: Pied Beauty
poems.author: hopkins
poems.ref: Poems of Gerard Manley Hopkins (ed. Robert Bridges, 1918), No. 13
poems.context: A “curtal” (shortened) sonnet praising everything spotted, mixed and strange. Hopkins’s poems were printed only in 1918, long after his death, by his friend Robert Bridges. Listen to the pile of sounds: “fickle, freckled”, “swift, slow; sweet, sour”. Text note: one long line that the printed page carried over (“…fold, fallow, and plough;”) is shown as a single line, as Hopkins wrote it.
poems.reflect: List five “pied” (mixed-colour) things you can see now.

poems.title: God’s Grandeur
poems.author: hopkins
poems.ref: Poems of Gerard Manley Hopkins (1918), No. 7
poems.context: The world is full of God’s energy, but industry has dirtied it (“seared with trade”). Still, nature renews itself. Read line 5 aloud: “have trod, have trod, have trod” — the sound of heavy feet. Text note: three long lines that the printed page carried over are shown as single lines, as Hopkins wrote them (14 lines).
poems.reflect: Find the line that sounds like walking. Why repeat it?

poems.title: Spring and Fall
poems.author: hopkins
poems.ref: Poems of Gerard Manley Hopkins (1918), No. 31

blight.en: a disease that kills plants; a curse

poems.context: An adult speaks to a child crying over falling leaves. She is really mourning — without knowing it — for herself, because everything that lives must end. Hopkins invents words (“unleaving”, “wanwood”).
poems.reflect: Why is Margaret really crying, according to the poem?
poems.text:
Margaret, are you grieving
Over Goldengrove unleaving?
Leaves, like the things of man, you
With your fresh thoughts care for, can you?
Ah! as the heart grows older
It will come to such sights colder
By and by, nor spare a sigh
Though worlds of wanwood leafmeal lie;
And yet you will weep and know why.
Now no matter, child, the name:
Sorrow's springs are the same.
Nor mouth had, no nor mind, expressed
What heart heard of, ghost guessed:
It is the blight man was born for,
It is Margaret you mourn for.

poems.title: Loveliest of Trees
poems.author: housman

threescore years and ten.en: seventy years (the old idea of a full life)

poems.context: A twenty-year-old calculates: seventy years of life minus twenty leaves fifty springs — not much time to look at cherry blossom. A favourite poem about enjoying the present. A good arithmetic puzzle for learners!
poems.reflect: Do the poet’s maths. Then write: “Now, of my ___ years…”.
poems.text:
Loveliest of trees, the cherry now
Is hung with bloom along the bough,
And stands about the woodland ride
Wearing white for Eastertide.

Now, of my threescore years and ten,
Twenty will not come again,
And take from seventy springs a score,
It only leaves me fifty more.

And since to look at things in bloom
Fifty springs are little room,
About the woodlands I will go
To see the cherry hung with snow.

poems.title: When I Was One-and-Twenty
poems.author: housman
poems.context: A young man ignores a wise man’s advice at twenty-one. At twenty-two, he knows it was true. Simple vocabulary, clear past tense, and a smile.
poems.reflect: What advice did you ignore and later understand? Begin “When I was …”.
poems.text:
When I was one-and-twenty
 I heard a wise man say,
"Give crowns and pounds and guineas
 But not your heart away;
Give pearls away and rubies
 But keep your fancy free."
But I was one-and-twenty,
 No use to talk to me.

When I was one-and-twenty
 I heard him say again,
"The heart out of the bosom
 Was never given in vain;
'Tis paid with sighs a plenty
 And sold for endless rue."
And I am two-and-twenty,
 And oh, 'tis true, 'tis true.

poems.title: If—
poems.author: kipling

impostors.en: people who pretend to be someone else

poems.context: A father’s advice to his son, in one long sentence of “if” clauses — 30 lines of conditions before the main clause (“Yours is the Earth…”) arrives in line 31. Kipling printed it in a book of stories, Rewards and Fairies. A perfect model of the first conditional.
poems.reflect: Write two lines of advice in Kipling’s pattern: “If you can …”.
poems.text:
If you can keep your head when all about you
Are losing theirs and blaming it on you;
If you can trust yourself when all men doubt you,
But make allowance for their doubting too;
If you can wait and not be tired by waiting,
Or being lied about, don’t deal in lies,
Or being hated, don’t give way to hating,
And yet don’t look too good, nor talk too wise;

If you can dream--and not make dreams your master;
If you can think--and not make thoughts your aim,
If you can meet with Triumph and Disaster
And treat those two impostors just the same;
If you can bear to hear the truth you’ve spoken
Twisted by knaves to make a trap for fools,
Or watch the things you gave your life to, broken,
And stoop and build ‘em up with worn-out tools;

If you can make one heap of all your winnings
And risk it on one turn of pitch-and-toss,
And lose, and start again at your beginnings
And never breathe a word about your loss;
If you can force your heart and nerve and sinew
To serve your turn long after they are gone,
And so hold on when there is nothing in you
Except the Will which says to them: ‘Hold on!’

If you can talk with crowds and keep your virtue,
Or walk with Kings--nor lose the common touch,
If neither foes nor loving friends can hurt you,
If all men count with you, but none too much;
If you can fill the unforgiving minute
With sixty seconds’ worth of distance run,
Yours is the Earth and everything that’s in it,
And--which is more--you’ll be a Man, my son!

poems.title: The Man He Killed
poems.author: hardy
poems.context: An ordinary soldier tries to explain why he shot a man who could have been his friend in a pub. Hardy writes in colloquial speech: “off-hand like”, “just as I”, “’list”. The pauses and dashes show a man struggling with his own reason.
poems.reflect: Find three colloquial (everyday spoken) expressions. Rewrite one in formal English.
poems.text:
"Had he and I but met
    By some old ancient inn,
We should have sat us down to wet
    Right many a nipperkin!

   "But ranged as infantry,
    And staring face to face,
I shot at him as he at me,
    And killed him in his place.

   "I shot him dead because--
    Because he was my foe,
Just so: my foe of course he was;
    That's clear enough; although

   "He thought he'd 'list, perhaps,
    Off-hand like--just as I--
Was out of work--had sold his traps--
    No other reason why.

   "Yes; quaint and curious war is!
    You shoot a fellow down
You'd treat, if met where any bar is,
    Or help to half-a-crown."

poems.title: In Time of “The Breaking of Nations”
poems.author: hardy

harrowing.en: breaking up soil with a farm tool

poems.context: Written during the First World War. Wars and dynasties pass; a man ploughing, a fire of weeds, two lovers — these will go on. The title quotes the Bible.
poems.reflect: Which everyday things in your country have stayed the same for centuries?
poems.text:
Only a man harrowing clods
  In a slow silent walk,
With an old horse that stumbles and nods
  Half asleep as they stalk.

Only thin smoke without flame
  From the heaps of couch grass:
Yet this will go onward the same
  Though Dynasties pass.

Yonder a maid and her wight
  Come whispering by;
War's annals will fade into night
  Ere their story die.

poems.title: The Soldier
poems.author: brooke
poems.context: Rupert Brooke wrote this at the start of the First World War and died in 1915 on the way to Gallipoli. It is idealistic and patriotic — very different from later war poetry. Compare it with Hardy’s “The Man He Killed”.
poems.reflect: Compare Brooke and Hardy: which poem do you believe more? Why?
poems.text:
If I should die, think only this of me:
  That there's some corner of a foreign field
That is for ever England. There shall be
  In that rich earth a richer dust concealed;
A dust whom England bore, shaped, made aware,
  Gave, once, her flowers to love, her ways to roam,
A body of England's, breathing English air,
  Washed by the rivers, blest by suns of home.

And think, this heart, all evil shed away,
  A pulse in the eternal mind, no less
    Gives somewhere back the thoughts by England given;
Her sights and sounds; dreams happy as her day;
  And laughter, learnt of friends; and gentleness,
    In hearts at peace, under an English heaven.

shakespeare.title: Sonnet 29 (“When, in disgrace with Fortune and men’s eyes”)
shakespeare.speaker: The poet
shakespeare.context: Feeling a failure, the poet envies everyone — until he thinks of the person he loves, and his mood rises “like to the lark at break of day”. The turn comes at “Yet”.
shakespeare.reflect: Find the word where the mood changes. What changes it?
shakespeare.text:
When, in disgrace with Fortune and men’s eyes,
I all alone beweep my outcast state,
And trouble deaf heaven with my bootless cries,
And look upon myself, and curse my fate,
Wishing me like to one more rich in hope,
Featured like him, like him with friends possest,
Desiring this man’s art and that man’s scope,
With what I most enjoy contented least;
Yet in these thoughts myself almost despising--
Haply I think on thee: and then my state,
Like to the Lark at break of day arising
From sullen earth, sings hymns at Heaven’s gate;
  For thy sweet love rememb’red such wealth brings
  That then I scorn to change my state with Kings.

shakespeare.title: Sonnet 30 (“When to the Sessions of sweet silent thought”)
shakespeare.speaker: The poet

sessions.en: sittings of a court (metaphor for memory)

shakespeare.context: Memory is a law court; old griefs are debts paid again and again. The language of money and law runs through the poem — until the couplet cancels every debt.
shakespeare.text:
When to the Sessions of sweet silent thought
I summon up remembrance of things past,
I sigh the lack of many a thing I sought,
And with old woes new wail my dear time’s waste:
Then can I drown an eye, unused to flow,
For precious friends hid in death’s dateless night,
And weep afresh love’s long-since-cancell’d woe,
And moan th’ expense of many a vanish’d sight:
Then can I grieve at grievances foregone,
And heavily from woe to woe tell o’er
The sad account of fore-bemoanèd moan,
Which I new pay as if not paid before.
  But if the while I think on thee, dear friend,
  All losses are restored and sorrows end.

shakespeare.title: Sonnet 73 (“That time of year thou may’st in me behold”)
shakespeare.speaker: The poet

choirs.en: the part of a church where singers stand

shakespeare.context: Three images of ending, one in each quatrain: late autumn, twilight, a dying fire. Each is shorter in time than the last. The couplet turns to the listener: your love is stronger because you will lose me.
shakespeare.reflect: Choose your own image of “ending”. Write one line.
shakespeare.text:
That time of year thou may’st in me behold
When yellow leaves, or none, or few, do hang
Upon those boughs which shake against the cold--
Bare ruin’d choirs where late the sweet birds sang.
In me thou see’st the twilight of such day
As after Sunset fadeth in the West,
Which by and by black night doth take away,
Death’s second self, that seals up all in rest.
In me thou see’st the glowing of such fire
That on the ashes of his youth doth lie,
As the death-bed whereon it must expire,
Consumed with that which it was nourish’d by.
  This thou perceiv’st, which makes thy love more strong
  To love that well which thou must leave ere long.

shakespeare.title: Sonnet 116 (“Let me not to the marriage of true minds”)
shakespeare.speaker: The poet

impediments.en: obstacles (an echo of the marriage service)

shakespeare.context: A definition of true love by what it is not. Love is a fixed star that guides lost ships. Often read at weddings. The final couplet bets everything: if I am wrong, no one has ever loved.
shakespeare.reflect: Write your own definition: “Love is not … / It is …”.
shakespeare.text:
Let me not to the marriage of true minds
Admit impediments. Love is not love
Which alters when it alteration finds,
Or bends with the remover to remove:
O, no! it is an ever-fixèd mark,
That looks on tempests and is never shaken;
It is the star to every wand’ring bark,
Whose worth’s unknown, although his height be taken.
Love’s not Time’s fool, though rosy lips and cheeks
Within his bending sickle’s compass come;
Love alters not with his brief hours and weeks,
But bears it out even to the edge of doom:--
  If this be error and upon me proved,
  I never writ, nor no man ever loved.

shakespeare.title: Sonnet 104 (“To me, fair friend, you never can be old”)
shakespeare.speaker: The poet
shakespeare.context: Three years have passed since the poet first saw his friend: three winters, three springs, three summers. Beauty moves away as slowly as a clock hand — you cannot see it move.
shakespeare.text:
To me, fair friend, you never can be old;
For as you were when first your eye I eyed,
Such seems your beauty still. Three Winters cold
Have from the forests shook three Summers’ pride;
Three beauteous springs to yellow Autumn turn’d
In process of the seasons have I seen,
Three April perfumes in three hot Junes burn’d,
Since first I saw you fresh, which yet are green,
Ah! yet doth beauty, like a dial-hand,
Steal from his figure, and no pace perceived;
So your sweet hue, which methinks still doth stand,
Hath motion, and mine eye may be deceived:
  For fear of which, hear this, thou age unbred:
  Ere you were born was beauty’s summer dead.

shakespeare.title: Sonnet 130 (“My mistress’ eyes are nothing like the sun”)
shakespeare.speaker: The poet

damask'd.en: with mixed red and white colour

reeks.en: here: comes out (in Shakespeare’s time not yet “smells bad”)

shakespeare.context: A joke against the poetic clichés of the time: eyes like the sun, lips like coral, cheeks like roses. His lover is a real woman — and that is why the love is real. Teacher note: the comparisons are frank and physical.
shakespeare.reflect: Write two honest, unpoetic compliments about something you love.
shakespeare.text:
My mistress' eyes are nothing like the sun;
Coral is far more red, than her lips red:
If snow be white, why then her breasts are dun;
If hairs be wires, black wires grow on her head.
I have seen roses damask'd, red and white,
But no such roses see I in her cheeks;
And in some perfumes is there more delight
Than in the breath that from my mistress reeks.
I love to hear her speak, yet well I know
That music hath a far more pleasing sound:
I grant I never saw a goddess go,--
My mistress, when she walks, treads on the ground:
  And yet by heaven, I think my love as rare,
  As any she belied with false compare.

shakespeare.title: Come unto these yellow sands
shakespeare.ref: Act I, Scene II · OBEV No. 129
shakespeare.speaker: Ariel, a spirit

Court’sied.en: curtsied: bent the knees in greeting

shakespeare.context: The invisible spirit Ariel sings to draw the shipwrecked Ferdinand across the island. Animal sounds (“Bow, wow”, “Cock-a-diddle-dow”) are part of the song.
shakespeare.text:
Come unto these yellow sands,
  And then take hands:
Court’sied when you have, and kiss’d,--
  The wild waves whist,--
Foot it featly here and there;
And, sweet sprites, the burthen bear.
      Hark, hark!
        Bow, wow,
      The watch-dogs bark.
        Bow, wow.
      Hark, hark! I hear
  The strain of strutting chanticleer
  Cry, Cock-a-diddle-dow!

shakespeare.title: Full fathom five
shakespeare.ref: Act I, Scene II · OBEV No. 131
shakespeare.speaker: Ariel, a spirit

fathom.en: a measure of depth: about 1.8 metres

sea-change.en: a change made by the sea; now any complete change

knell.en: the sound of a funeral bell

shakespeare.context: Ariel sings to Ferdinand that his father lies drowned (in fact King Alonso is alive) and has been turned into coral and pearls. The phrase “sea-change” is now everyday English for a complete transformation (see Everyday English from Shakespeare).
shakespeare.text:
Full fathom five thy father lies;
  Of his bones are coral made;
Those are pearls that were his eyes:
  Nothing of him that doth fade,
But doth suffer a sea-change
Into something rich and strange.
Sea-nymphs hourly ring his knell:
                        Ding-dong.
  Hark! now I hear them--
            Ding-dong, bell!

shakespeare.title: Blow, blow, thou winter wind
shakespeare.ref: Act II, Scene VII · OBEV No. 136
shakespeare.speaker: Amiens, a lord
shakespeare.context: In the Forest of Arden, a courtier sings that winter is less cruel than human ingratitude. The refrain “Then heigh ho, the holly!” lightens the mood.
shakespeare.text:
Blow, blow, thou winter wind,
Thou art not so unkind
  As man’s ingratitude;
Thy tooth is not so keen,
Because thou art not seen,
  Although thy breath be rude.
Heigh ho! sing, heigh ho! unto the green holly:
Most friendship is feigning, most loving mere folly:
          Then heigh ho, the holly!
          This life is most jolly.

        Freeze, freeze, thou bitter sky,
        That dost not bite so nigh
          As benefits forgot:
        Though thou the waters warp,
        Thy sting is not so sharp
          As friend remember’d not.
Heigh ho! sing, heigh ho! unto the green holly:
Most friendship is feigning, most loving mere folly:
          Then heigh ho, the holly!
          This life is most jolly.

shakespeare.title: Friends, Romans, countrymen
shakespeare.speaker: Mark Antony
shakespeare.context: The most famous persuasive speech in English drama. Antony says he will not praise Caesar — and then turns the crowd against Brutus by repeating “Brutus is an honourable man” until the words mean the opposite.
shakespeare.reflect: How does the meaning of “honourable” change through the speech?
shakespeare.extractNote: Extract from the complete play text in Shakespeare’s World; nothing inside the lines shown has been changed.
shakespeare.text:
Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears;
I come to bury Caesar, not to praise him.
The evil that men do lives after them,
The good is oft interred with their bones;
So let it be with Caesar. The noble Brutus
Hath told you Caesar was ambitious.
If it were so, it was a grievous fault,
And grievously hath Caesar answer’d it.
Here, under leave of Brutus and the rest,
For Brutus is an honourable man,
So are they all, all honourable men,
Come I to speak in Caesar’s funeral.
He was my friend, faithful and just to me;
But Brutus says he was ambitious,
And Brutus is an honourable man.
He hath brought many captives home to Rome,
Whose ransoms did the general coffers fill:
Did this in Caesar seem ambitious?
When that the poor have cried, Caesar hath wept;
Ambition should be made of sterner stuff:
Yet Brutus says he was ambitious;
And Brutus is an honourable man.
You all did see that on the Lupercal
I thrice presented him a kingly crown,
Which he did thrice refuse. Was this ambition?
Yet Brutus says he was ambitious;
And sure he is an honourable man.
I speak not to disprove what Brutus spoke,
But here I am to speak what I do know.
You all did love him once, not without cause;
What cause withholds you then to mourn for him?
O judgement, thou art fled to brutish beasts,
And men have lost their reason. Bear with me.
My heart is in the coffin there with Caesar,
And I must pause till it come back to me.

shakespeare.title: Once more unto the breach
shakespeare.speaker: King Henry

breach.en: a gap in a wall made in battle

shakespeare.context: Henry urges his soldiers back into the attack at Harfleur. Notice the imperatives (“imitate”, “stiffen”, “summon up”) — a model of motivational speech.
shakespeare.reflect: List five imperatives. Which is the strongest?
shakespeare.extractNote: Extract from the complete play text in Shakespeare’s World; nothing inside the lines shown has been changed.
shakespeare.text:
Once more unto the breach, dear friends, once more,
Or close the wall up with our English dead.
In peace there’s nothing so becomes a man
As modest stillness and humility;
But when the blast of war blows in our ears,
Then imitate the action of the tiger;
Stiffen the sinews, summon up the blood,
Disguise fair nature with hard-favour’d rage;
Then lend the eye a terrible aspect;
Let it pry through the portage of the head
Like the brass cannon; let the brow o’erwhelm it
As fearfully as does a galled rock
O’erhang and jutty his confounded base,
Swill’d with the wild and wasteful ocean.
Now set the teeth and stretch the nostril wide,
Hold hard the breath, and bend up every spirit
To his full height. On, on, you noblest English,
Whose blood is fet from fathers of war-proof!
Fathers that, like so many Alexanders,
Have in these parts from morn till even fought,
And sheath’d their swords for lack of argument.
Dishonour not your mothers; now attest
That those whom you call’d fathers did beget you.
Be copy now to men of grosser blood,
And teach them how to war. And you, good yeomen,
Whose limbs were made in England, show us here
The mettle of your pasture; let us swear
That you are worth your breeding, which I doubt not;
For there is none of you so mean and base,
That hath not noble lustre in your eyes.
I see you stand like greyhounds in the slips,
Straining upon the start. The game’s afoot!
Follow your spirit, and upon this charge
Cry, “God for Harry! England and Saint George!”

shakespeare.title: We few, we happy few (St Crispin’s Day)
shakespeare.speaker: King Henry

vigil.en: the evening before a holy day

shakespeare.context: Before the battle of Agincourt, outnumbered, Henry promises his men that this day will be remembered for ever — and that those who fight will be his brothers. “Band of brothers” is now everyday English.
shakespeare.reflect: Why does Henry say “the fewer men, the greater share of honour”? Agree or disagree.
shakespeare.extractNote: Extract from the complete play text in Shakespeare’s World; nothing inside the lines shown has been changed.
shakespeare.text:
This day is call’d the feast of Crispian.
He that outlives this day, and comes safe home,
Will stand a tip-toe when this day is named,
And rouse him at the name of Crispian.
He that shall live this day, and see old age,
Will yearly on the vigil feast his neighbours,
And say, “Tomorrow is Saint Crispian.”
Then will he strip his sleeve and show his scars,
And say, “These wounds I had on Crispian’s day.”
Old men forget; yet all shall be forgot,
But he’ll remember with advantages
What feats he did that day. Then shall our names,
Familiar in his mouth as household words,
Harry the King, Bedford, and Exeter,
Warwick and Talbot, Salisbury and Gloucester,
Be in their flowing cups freshly remembered.
This story shall the good man teach his son;
And Crispin Crispian shall ne’er go by,
From this day to the ending of the world,
But we in it shall be remembered,
We few, we happy few, we band of brothers.
For he today that sheds his blood with me
Shall be my brother; be he ne’er so vile,
This day shall gentle his condition;
And gentlemen in England now abed
Shall think themselves accurs’d they were not here,
And hold their manhoods cheap whiles any speaks
That fought with us upon Saint Crispin’s day.

shakespeare.title: Is this a dagger which I see before me
shakespeare.speaker: Macbeth
shakespeare.context: Alone, before he murders King Duncan, Macbeth sees a dagger floating in the air. A soliloquy: the audience hears a mind in crisis.
shakespeare.extractNote: Extract from the complete play text in Shakespeare’s World; nothing inside the lines shown has been changed.
shakespeare.text:
Is this a dagger which I see before me,
The handle toward my hand? Come, let me clutch thee:—
I have thee not, and yet I see thee still.
Art thou not, fatal vision, sensible
To feeling as to sight? or art thou but
A dagger of the mind, a false creation,
Proceeding from the heat-oppressed brain?
I see thee yet, in form as palpable
As this which now I draw.
Thou marshall’st me the way that I was going;
And such an instrument I was to use.
Mine eyes are made the fools o’ the other senses,
Or else worth all the rest: I see thee still;
And on thy blade and dudgeon, gouts of blood,
Which was not so before.—There’s no such thing.
It is the bloody business which informs
Thus to mine eyes.—Now o’er the one half-world
Nature seems dead, and wicked dreams abuse
The curtain’d sleep. Witchcraft celebrates
Pale Hecate’s off’rings; and wither’d murder,
Alarum’d by his sentinel, the wolf,
Whose howl’s his watch, thus with his stealthy pace,
With Tarquin’s ravishing strides, towards his design
Moves like a ghost.—Thou sure and firm-set earth,
Hear not my steps, which way they walk, for fear
Thy very stones prate of my whereabout,
And take the present horror from the time,
Which now suits with it.—Whiles I threat, he lives.
Words to the heat of deeds too cold breath gives.

shakespeare.title: Fair is foul, and foul is fair
shakespeare.speaker: The three Witches
shakespeare.context: The witches’ chant at the very start of the play. It warns us: in this play, nothing is what it seems.
shakespeare.reflect: Give an example from life where something “fair” was really “foul”.
shakespeare.extractNote: Extract from the complete play text in Shakespeare’s World; nothing inside the lines shown has been changed.
shakespeare.text:
Fair is foul, and foul is fair:
Hover through the fog and filthy air.

shakespeare.title: Out, damned spot!
shakespeare.speaker: Lady Macbeth (sleepwalking)
shakespeare.context: Lady Macbeth walks in her sleep and tries to wash invisible blood from her hands. The speech is in prose, broken and confused — guilt has destroyed her control.
shakespeare.extractNote: Extract from the complete play text in Shakespeare’s World; nothing inside the lines shown has been changed.
shakespeare.text: Out, damned spot! out, I say! One; two. Why, then ’tis time to do’t. Hell is murky! Fie, my lord, fie! a soldier, and afeard? What need we fear who knows it, when none can call our power to account? Yet who would have thought the old man to have had so much blood in him?

shakespeare.title: Will all great Neptune’s ocean wash this blood
shakespeare.speaker: Macbeth

Neptune.en: the Roman god of the sea

shakespeare.context: Just after the murder. Compare the long Latin word “multitudinous … incarnadine” with the simple English “making the green one red” — Shakespeare says the same thing twice in two kinds of English.
shakespeare.extractNote: Extract from the complete play text in Shakespeare’s World; nothing inside the lines shown has been changed.
shakespeare.text:
Will all great Neptune’s ocean wash this blood
Clean from my hand? No, this my hand will rather
The multitudinous seas incarnadine,
Making the green one red.

shakespeare.title: What a piece of work is man
shakespeare.speaker: Hamlet
shakespeare.context: Hamlet praises humanity in magnificent prose — and then says it means nothing to him. A portrait of depression; introduce with care.
shakespeare.extractNote: Extract from the complete play text in Shakespeare’s World; nothing inside the lines shown has been changed.
shakespeare.text: What a piece of work is man, how noble in reason, how infinite in faculties, in form and moving, how express and admirable; in action how like an angel, in apprehension, how like a god: the beauty of the world, the paragon of animals. And yet, to me, what is this quintessence of dust?

shakespeare.title: This royal throne of kings, this sceptered isle
shakespeare.speaker: John of Gaunt

sceptered.en: ruled by kings (a sceptre is a royal staff)

shakespeare.context: A dying man’s praise of England: one long list of “this …” phrases, building to the final word. Count them!
shakespeare.extractNote: Extract from the complete play text in Shakespeare’s World; nothing inside the lines shown has been changed.
shakespeare.text:
This royal throne of kings, this sceptered isle,
This earth of majesty, this seat of Mars,
This other Eden, demi-paradise,
This fortress built by Nature for herself
Against infection and the hand of war,
This happy breed of men, this little world,
This precious stone set in the silver sea,
Which serves it in the office of a wall
Or as a moat defensive to a house,
Against the envy of less happier lands;
This blessed plot, this earth, this realm, this England,

shakespeare.title: But soft, what light through yonder window breaks?
shakespeare.speaker: Romeo

spheres.en: the orbits of stars and planets

shakespeare.context: The balcony scene. Romeo sees Juliet at her window and, unheard by her, compares her to the sun and her eyes to stars. Read it in its scene in the complete play.
shakespeare.extractNote: Extract from the complete play text in Shakespeare’s World; nothing inside the lines shown has been changed.
shakespeare.text:
But soft, what light through yonder window breaks?
It is the east, and Juliet is the sun!
Arise fair sun and kill the envious moon,
Who is already sick and pale with grief,
That thou her maid art far more fair than she.
Be not her maid since she is envious;
Her vestal livery is but sick and green,
And none but fools do wear it; cast it off.
It is my lady, O it is my love!
O, that she knew she were!
She speaks, yet she says nothing. What of that?
Her eye discourses, I will answer it.
I am too bold, ’tis not to me she speaks.
Two of the fairest stars in all the heaven,
Having some business, do entreat her eyes
To twinkle in their spheres till they return.
What if her eyes were there, they in her head?
The brightness of her cheek would shame those stars,
As daylight doth a lamp; her eyes in heaven
Would through the airy region stream so bright
That birds would sing and think it were not night.
See how she leans her cheek upon her hand.
O that I were a glove upon that hand,
That I might touch that cheek.

shakespeare.title: I know a bank where the wild thyme blows
shakespeare.speaker: Oberon, King of the Fairies
shakespeare.context: Oberon describes where Titania sleeps. A catalogue of English wild flowers in iambic pentameter.
shakespeare.extractNote: Extract from the complete play text in Shakespeare’s World; nothing inside the lines shown has been changed.
shakespeare.text:
I know a bank where the wild thyme blows,
Where oxlips and the nodding violet grows,
Quite over-canopied with luscious woodbine,
With sweet musk-roses, and with eglantine.
There sleeps Titania sometime of the night,
Lull’d in these flowers with dances and delight;
And there the snake throws her enamell’d skin,
Weed wide enough to wrap a fairy in.

shakespeare.title: Be not afeard. The isle is full of noises
shakespeare.speaker: Caliban
shakespeare.context: Caliban, treated as a monster, speaks some of the most beautiful lines in the play: the island’s music makes him cry to dream again.
shakespeare.extractNote: Extract from the complete play text in Shakespeare’s World; nothing inside the lines shown has been changed.
shakespeare.text:
Be not afeard. The isle is full of noises,
Sounds, and sweet airs, that give delight, and hurt not.
Sometimes a thousand twangling instruments
Will hum about mine ears; and sometimes voices,
That, if I then had wak’d after long sleep,
Will make me sleep again: and then, in dreaming,
The clouds methought would open and show riches
Ready to drop upon me; that, when I wak’d,
I cried to dream again.

shakespeare.title: Blow, winds, and crack your cheeks!
shakespeare.speaker: King Lear
shakespeare.context: On the heath in a storm, Lear commands the weather to destroy the world. His language is as violent as the storm.
shakespeare.extractNote: Extract from the complete play text in Shakespeare’s World; nothing inside the lines shown has been changed.
shakespeare.text:
Blow, winds, and crack your cheeks! Rage! blow!
You cataracts and hurricanoes, spout
Till you have drench’d our steeples, drown’d the cocks!
You sulphurous and thought-executing fires,
Vaunt-couriers to oak-cleaving thunderbolts,
Singe my white head! And thou, all-shaking thunder,
Strike flat the thick rotundity o’ the world!
Crack nature’s moulds, all germens spill at once,
That make ingrateful man!

shakespeare.title: The barge she sat in, like a burnished throne
shakespeare.speaker: Enobarbus

poop.en: the back deck of a ship

shakespeare.context: A soldier describes the first meeting of Antony and Cleopatra. Shakespeare took the details from Plutarch, in Thomas North’s translation — and turned them into verse.
shakespeare.extractNote: Extract from the complete play text in Shakespeare’s World; nothing inside the lines shown has been changed.
shakespeare.text:
The barge she sat in, like a burnished throne,
Burned on the water. The poop was beaten gold;
Purple the sails, and so perfumed that
The winds were love-sick with them; the oars were silver,
Which to the tune of flutes kept stroke, and made
The water which they beat to follow faster,
As amorous of their strokes. For her own person,
It beggared all description: she did lie
In her pavilion, cloth-of-gold of tissue,
O’erpicturing that Venus where we see
The fancy outwork nature. On each side her

shakespeare.title: Uneasy lies the head that wears a crown
shakespeare.speaker: King Henry IV
shakespeare.context: The tired king cannot sleep while the poorest of his subjects can. The line became a proverb about the worries of power.
shakespeare.extractNote: The last line of a longer speech, quoted exactly from the complete play.
shakespeare.text: Uneasy lies the head that wears a crown.

proverbs.text: Beggars must not be choosers.

meaning.en: If you are asking for help, you cannot be fussy about what you get.
meaning.ru: Дарёному коню в зубы не смотрят.

proverbs.use: Someone gives you an old bike for free. What would you say if you complained?

proverbs.text: Well begun is half done.

meaning.en: A good start makes the rest of the job much easier.

proverbs.use: Describe the first step of a project you started well.

proverbs.text: Take care of the pence, and the pounds will take care of themselves.

meaning.en: If you are careful with small amounts of money, the big amounts will look after themselves.

proverbs.use: Give one small saving you could make every day.

proverbs.text: Charity begins at home.

meaning.en: You should help your own family and people close to you first.
meaning.ru: Своя рубашка ближе к телу; милосердие начинается дома.

proverbs.use: Do you agree? When should we help strangers first?

proverbs.text: Civil words cost nothing, and go a long way.

meaning.en: Being polite costs you nothing and helps a lot.
meaning.ru: Вежливость ничего не стоит, а ценится дорого.

proverbs.use: Write two polite phrases that “go a long way” in English.

proverbs.text: What cannot be cured must be endured.

meaning.en: If you cannot change a bad situation, you must accept it.
meaning.ru: Чему быть, того не миновать; что нельзя исправить, надо терпеть.

proverbs.use: Name a situation where this is good advice — and one where it is not.

proverbs.text: Talk of the devil and he'll be sure to appear.

meaning.en: Said when the person you are talking about suddenly appears. (Today: “Speak of the devil!”)

proverbs.use: Use the modern short form in a dialogue: “Speak of the devil!”

proverbs.text: A drowning man will catch at a straw.

meaning.en: A person in great trouble will try anything, even something useless.

proverbs.use: Compare with the Russian and Kazakh proverbs. Are the images the same?

proverbs.text: Little pitchers have long ears.

meaning.en: Children hear more than adults think — be careful what you say near them.
meaning.ru: У маленьких кувшинов большие уши (дети всё слышат).

proverbs.use: When might a parent use this proverb?

proverbs.text: Don't put all your eggs into one basket.

meaning.en: Do not risk everything on one plan.
meaning.ru: Не клади все яйца в одну корзину.

proverbs.use: Give advice to a friend who is applying to only one university.

proverbs.text: Empty vessels make the greatest sound.

meaning.en: People who talk the most often know the least.

proverbs.use: Do you know someone like this? Describe them politely.

proverbs.text: Enough is as good as a feast.

meaning.en: Having enough is as good as having a lot.

proverbs.use: What is “enough” for you? Answer in two sentences.

proverbs.text: Example teaches more than precept.

meaning.en: People learn more from what you do than from what you say.

proverbs.use: Tell about a person whose example taught you something.

proverbs.text: Familiarity breeds contempt.

meaning.en: When you know someone too well, you can stop respecting them.

proverbs.use: Do you agree? Give an example from work or family life.

proverbs.text: Fine feathers make fine birds.

meaning.en: Fine clothes make people look important (but do not change who they are).

proverbs.use: Is this true at job interviews? Discuss.

proverbs.text: First come, first served.

meaning.en: People who come first will be helped first.
meaning.ru: Кто первый пришёл, того первым и обслужили.

proverbs.use: Where have you seen a “first come, first served” rule?

proverbs.text: Forewarned is forearmed.

meaning.en: If you know about a danger in advance, you can prepare for it.

proverbs.use: What warning helped you prepare for something?

proverbs.text: Fortune favours the brave.

meaning.en: Success comes to people who are brave and take risks.

proverbs.use: Tell about a time when courage helped you.

proverbs.text: Out of the frying-pan into the fire.

meaning.en: From a bad situation into a worse one.

proverbs.use: Describe a situation that went “out of the frying-pan into the fire”.

proverbs.text: Those who live in glass houses should not throw stones.

meaning.en: Do not criticise others for faults that you have yourself.
meaning.ru: Не суди, да не судим будешь.
meaning.kz: Өз кемшілігің бола тұра, өзгені сынама.

proverbs.use: Rewrite the proverb as advice in modern words.

proverbs.text: All that glitters is not gold.

meaning.en: Things that look valuable are not always valuable. (Shakespeare wrote “glisters”.)
meaning.ru: Не всё то золото, что блестит.

proverbs.use: Find Shakespeare’s version in Shakespeare’s World: “All that glisters is not gold”.

proverbs.text: One good turn deserves another.

meaning.en: If someone helps you, you should help them in return.
meaning.ru: Долг платежом красен; услуга за услугу.

proverbs.use: Tell about a good turn you returned.

proverbs.text: More haste worse speed.

meaning.en: If you do things too quickly, you make mistakes and lose time. (Today: “More haste, less speed”.)

proverbs.use: When did hurrying cost you time?

proverbs.text: Do not holloa till you are out of the wood.

meaning.en: Do not celebrate before you are really safe. (Today: “Don’t count your chickens…” has a similar meaning.)

proverbs.use: Compare with proverb 237 in this collection.

proverbs.text: Hunger is the finest sauce.

meaning.en: When you are very hungry, any food tastes good.

proverbs.use: Describe a meal that tasted wonderful because you were hungry.

proverbs.text: Many a true word is spoken in jest.

meaning.en: People often say true things while pretending to joke.
meaning.ru: В каждой шутке есть доля правды.

proverbs.use: Has a joke ever told you something true?

proverbs.text: Knowledge is power.

meaning.en: The more you know, the more you can do.

proverbs.use: How has knowledge given you “power” in a situation?

proverbs.text: It is the last straw that breaks the camel's back.

meaning.en: A small problem can be too much when added to many others.

proverbs.use: What was the “last straw” in a story you know?

proverbs.text: Never too old to learn.

meaning.en: You can learn new things at any age.

proverbs.use: Name someone who started learning something late in life.

proverbs.text: Least said is soonest mended.

meaning.en: Saying less in a difficult situation makes it easier to repair.

proverbs.use: Give advice to two friends after an argument.

proverbs.text: While there's life there's hope.

meaning.en: As long as someone is alive, things can still get better.

proverbs.use: Write a message of hope to a friend.

proverbs.text: Like father like son.

meaning.en: Sons are often similar to their fathers.

proverbs.use: In what ways are you like your parents?

proverbs.text: Live and learn.

meaning.en: You learn new things all through your life, often from mistakes.

proverbs.use: Tell about something you learned recently by surprise.

proverbs.text: The more the merrier; the fewer the better cheer.

meaning.en: The more people come, the more fun it is. (Preston adds the opposite view!)

proverbs.use: Preston’s entry has two halves that disagree. Which half do you prefer?

proverbs.text: In for a penny, in for a pound.

meaning.en: If you have started something, you may as well go all the way.

proverbs.use: When is it wise — and unwise — to follow this proverb?

proverbs.text: Penny wise and pound foolish.

meaning.en: Careful with small sums but careless with large ones.

proverbs.use: Give a modern example of being “penny wise and pound foolish”.

proverbs.text: Prevention is better than cure.

meaning.en: It is better to stop a problem before it starts than to fix it later.

proverbs.use: Give one example from health and one from technology.

proverbs.text: The proof of the pudding is in the eating.

meaning.en: You can only judge something by trying it.

proverbs.use: What did you judge wrongly before you tried it?

proverbs.text: It never rains but it pours.
proverbs.use: Tell about a day when everything went wrong at once.

proverbs.text: When you are at Rome, do as Rome does.

meaning.en: When you are in another place, follow the customs of the people there. (Today: “When in Rome…”)
meaning.ru: В чужой монастырь со своим уставом не ходят.
meaning.kz: Басқа елде сол елдің салтымен жүр.

proverbs.use: Give advice to a visitor to your city.

proverbs.text: Seeing is believing.

meaning.en: People believe something only when they see it.
meaning.ru: Лучше один раз увидеть, чем сто раз услышать.
meaning.kz: Мың рет естігенше, бір рет көр.

proverbs.use: What did you not believe until you saw it?

proverbs.text: Don't wake a sleeping dog.

meaning.en: Do not start trouble that has gone quiet. (Today: “Let sleeping dogs lie”.)
meaning.ru: Не буди лихо, пока оно тихо.

proverbs.use: When is it better not to talk about an old problem?

proverbs.text: Where there is smoke there is fire.

meaning.en: If people are talking about a problem, there is probably some truth in it.

proverbs.use: Is this proverb fair to people who are the subject of rumours?

proverbs.text: Don't cut your nose off to spite your face.

meaning.en: Do not hurt yourself just because you are angry with someone else.

proverbs.use: Describe someone who “cut off their nose to spite their face”.

proverbs.text: Little strokes fell great oaks.

meaning.en: Many small efforts achieve great results. (Benjamin Franklin uses it too.)

proverbs.use: Find the same words in Franklin’s The Way to Wealth (Sayings born in books).

proverbs.text: One swallow does not make a summer.

meaning.en: One good sign does not mean that everything is now good.

proverbs.use: Give an example from sport or the economy.

proverbs.text: Think twice before you speak once.

meaning.en: Think carefully before you say something.
meaning.ru: Семь раз отмерь, один раз отрежь (о словах).

proverbs.use: When did you wish you had thought twice?

proverbs.text: Truth is stranger than fiction.

meaning.en: Real events can be stranger than invented stories. (Byron wrote a famous version of it.)

proverbs.use: Tell a true story that sounds invented.

proverbs.text: If wishes were horses, beggars would ride.

meaning.en: Wishing does not make things happen.
meaning.kz: Тілек атқа айналса, кедей мінер еді.

proverbs.use: What would you do if wishes were horses?

proverbs.text: Two wrongs will not make a right.

meaning.en: Doing something bad to someone who hurt you does not make the situation right.

proverbs.use: Explain this proverb to a younger child.

proverbs.text: An honest man's word is as good as his bond.

meaning.en: An honest person keeps promises as if they were written contracts.

proverbs.use: What promises do you always keep?
