limericks.title: There was a Young Lady of Ryde
limericks.text:
There was a Young Lady of Ryde,
Whose shoe-strings were seldom untied;
She purchased some clogs,
And some small spotty dogs,
And frequently walked about Ryde.

limericks.title: There was an Old Man with a nose
limericks.text:
There was an Old Man with a nose,
Who said, "If you choose to suppose,
That my nose is too long,
You are certainly wrong!"
That remarkable Man with a nose.

limericks.title: There was a Young Lady whose chin
limericks.text:
There was a Young Lady whose chin,
Resembled the point of a pin:
So she had it made sharp,
And purchased a harp,
And played several tunes with her chin.

limericks.title: There was a Young Lady of Portugal
limericks.text:
There was a Young lady of Portugal,
Whose ideas were excessively nautical;
She climbed up a tree,
To examine the sea,
But declared she would never leave Portugal.

limericks.title: There was an Old Man of the Isles
limericks.text:
There was an Old Man of the Isles,
Whose face was pervaded with smiles;
He sung high dum diddle,
And played on the fiddle,
That amiable Man of the Isles.

limericks.title: There was an Old Man of the West
limericks.text:
There was an Old Man of the West,
Who wore a pale plum-coloured vest;
When they said, "Does it fit?"
He replied, "Not a bit!"
That uneasy Old Man of the West.

limericks.title: There was a Young Lady whose nose
limericks.text:
There was a Young Lady whose nose,
Was so long that it reached to her toes;
So she hired an Old Lady,
Whose conduct was steady,
To carry that wonderful nose.

limericks.title: There was an Old Man of the Hague
limericks.text:
There was an Old Man of the Hague,
Whose ideas were excessively vague;
He built a balloon,
To examine the moon,
That deluded Old Man of the Hague.

limericks.title: There was an Old Man who said, “Hush!”
limericks.text:
There was an Old Man who said, "Hush!
I perceive a young bird in this bush!"
When they said--"Is it small?"
He replied--"Not at all!
It is four times as big as the bush!"

limericks.title: There was an Old Man of the Coast
limericks.text:
There was an Old Man of the Coast,
Who placidly sat on a post;
But when it was cold,
He relinquished his hold,
And called for some hot buttered toast.

limericks.title: There was an Old Man, who said, “Well!”
limericks.text:
There was an Old Man, who said, "Well!
Will NOBODY answer this bell?
I have pulled day and night,
Till my hair has grown white,
But nobody answers this bell!"

limericks.title: There was a Young Lady of Wales
limericks.text:
There was a Young Lady of Wales,
Who caught a large fish without scales;
When she lifted her hook,
She exclaimed, "Only look!"
That ecstatic Young Lady of Wales.

limericks.title: There was an Old Person of Gretna
limericks.text:
There was an Old Person of Gretna,
Who rushed down the crater of Etna;
When they said, "Is it hot?"
He replied, "No, it's not!"
That mendacious Old Person of Gretna.

limericks.title: There was an old Person of Burton
limericks.text:
There was an old Person of Burton,
Whose answers were rather uncertain;
When they said, "How d'ye do?"
He replied, "Who are you?"
That distressing old person of Burton.

limericks.title: There was an Old Man, on whose nose
limericks.text:
There was an Old Man, on whose nose,
Most birds of the air could repose;
But they all flew away,
At the closing of day,
Which relieved that Old Man and his nose.

riddles.title: There was a girl in our towne
riddles.text:
There was a girl in our towne,
Silk an' satin was her gowne,
Silk an' satin, gold an' velvet,
Guess her name, three times I've tell'd it.

riddles.title: I went to the wood and got it
riddles.text:
I went to the wood and got it,
I sat me down and looked at it;
The more I looked at it the less I liked it,
And I brought it home because I couldn't help it.

riddles.title: When I was taken from the fair body
riddles.text:
When I was taken from the fair body,
  They then cut off my head,
  And thus my shape was altered;
It's I that make peace between king and king,
  And many a true lover glad:
All this I do and ten times more,
  And more I could do still,
But nothing can I do,
  Without my guider's will.

riddles.title: As I was going o’er London Bridge
riddles.text:
As I was going o'er London Bridge,
I met a cart full of fingers and thumbs!

riddles.title: As soft as silk, as white as milk
riddles.text:
As soft as silk, as white as milk,
As bitter as gall, a thick wall,
And a green coat covers me all.

riddles.title: Humpty Dumpty lay in a beck
riddles.text:
Humpty Dumpty lay in a beck,[*]
With all his sinews round his neck;
Forty doctors and forty wrights
Couldn't put Humpty Dumpty to rights!

riddles.title: I have a little sister, they call her peep, peep
In marble walls as white as milk
riddles.text:
In marble walls as white as milk,
Lined with a skin as soft as silk;
Within a fountain crystal clear,
A golden apple doth appear.
No doors there are to this strong-hold.
Yet things break in and steal the gold.

riddles.title: Little Nancy Etticoat
riddles.text:
Little Nancy Etticoat,
In a white petticoat,
And a red nose;
The longer she stands,
The shorter she grows.

riddles.title: Long legs, crooked thighs
riddles.text:
Long legs, crooked thighs,
Little head and no eyes.

riddles.title: Old mother Twitchett had but one eye
riddles.text:
Old mother Twitchett had but one eye,
And a long tail which she let fly;
And every time she went over a gap,
She left a bit of her tail in a trap.

grose.head: BUCKET
grose.entry: BUCKET. To kick the bucket; to die.
grose.note: Still used: “to kick the bucket” = to die (informal, joking).

grose.head: BROWN STUDY
grose.entry: BROWN STUDY. Said of one absent, in a reverie, or thoughtful.
grose.note: Still used, rather literary: “in a brown study” = lost in thought.

grose.head: BLUE DEVILS
grose.entry: BLUE DEVILS. Low spirits.
grose.note: Survives as “the blues” (sadness; also the music).

grose.head: BACON
grose.entry: BACON. He has saved his bacon; he has escaped. He has a good voice to beg bacon; a saying in ridicule of a bad voice.
grose.note: Still used: “to save someone’s bacon” = to rescue them.

grose.head: BREAD BASKET
grose.entry: BREAD BASKET. The stomach; a term used by boxers. I took him a punch in his bread basket; i.e. I gave him a blow in the stomach.
grose.note: Still understood as a joke word for the stomach.

grose.head: BUBBLE AND SQUEAK
grose.entry: BUBBLE AND SQUEAK. Beef and cabbage fried together. It is so called from its bubbling up and squeaking whilst over the fire.
grose.note: Still a British dish (now usually potato and cabbage).

meaning.en: fried cabbage with meat or potato

grose.head: CHATTER BOX
grose.entry: CHATTER BOX. One whose tongue runs twelve score to the dozen, a chattering man or woman.
grose.note: Now one word: “chatterbox”.

meaning.en: a person who talks a lot

grose.head: COCK AND A BULL STORY
grose.entry: COCK AND A BULL STORY. A roundabout story, without head or tail, i.e. beginning or ending.
grose.note: Still used: “a cock-and-bull story” = an unbelievable excuse.

grose.head: DOG LATIN
grose.entry: DOG LATIN. Barbarous Latin, such as was formerly used by the lawyers in their pleadings.
grose.note: Still used for bad or fake Latin.

grose.head: DUDS
grose.entry: DUDS. Clothes.
grose.note: Still used informally for clothes.

grose.head: FIDDLE FADDLE
grose.entry: FIDDLE FADDLE. Trifling discourse, nonsense. A mere fiddle faddle fellow; a trifier.
grose.note: Old-fashioned today.

grose.head: FUDGE
grose.entry: FUDGE. Nonsense.
grose.note: Survives as a verb: “to fudge” the numbers = to make vague or dishonest.

grose.head: GRUB
grose.entry: GRUB. Victuals. To grub; to dine.
grose.note: Still informal for food — the Artful Dodger uses it in Oliver Twist.

grose.head: GRUB STREET
grose.entry: GRUB STREET. A street near Moorfields, formerly the supposed habitation of many persons who wrote for the booksellers: hence a Grub-street writer means a hackney author, who manufactures booss for the booksellers.
grose.note: Still used for low-quality hack writing.

grose.head: GULL
grose.entry: GULL. A simple credulous fellow, easily cheated.
grose.note: Survives in “gullible”. Shakespeare uses “gull” too.

grose.head: HUSH MONEY
grose.entry: HUSH MONEY. Money given to hush up or conceal a robbery, theft, or any other offence, or to take off the evidence from appearing against a criminal.
grose.note: Still used: money paid to keep someone quiet.

grose.head: JAW
grose.entry: JAW. Speech, discourse. Give us none of your jaw; let us have none of your discourse. A jaw-me-dead; a talkative fellow. Jaw work; a cry used in fairs by the sellers of nuts.
grose.note: Survives in “jaw” = a long talk, “jaw-jaw”.

grose.head: LARK
grose.entry: LARK. A boat.
grose.note: Still used: “for a lark” = for fun.

grose.head: LINGO
grose.entry: LINGO. Language. An outlandish lingo; a foreign tongue. The parlezvous lingo; the French language.
grose.note: Still used informally for a language or jargon.

grose.head: MOONSHINE
grose.entry: MOONSHINE. A matter or mouthful of moonshine; a trifle, nothing. The white brandy smuggled on the coasts of Kent and Sussex, and the gin in the north of Yorkshire, are also called moonshine.
grose.note: Both meanings survive: nonsense, and illegally made spirits.

grose.head: MUM
grose.entry: MUM. An interjection directing silence. Mum for that; I shall be silent as to that. As mute as Mumchance, who was hanged for saying nothing; a friendly reproach to any one who seems low-spirited and silent.
grose.note: Still used: “mum’s the word” = keep it secret.

grose.head: QUID
grose.entry: QUID. The quantity of tobacco put into the mouth at one time. To quid tobacco; to chew tobacco. Quid est hoc? hoc est quid; a guinea. Half a quid; half a guinea. The swell tipped me fifty quid for the prad; the gentleman gave fifty pounds for the horse.
grose.note: Still British slang for a pound (£1).

grose.head: QUIZ
grose.entry: QUIZ. A strange-looking fellow, an odd dog. OXFORD.
grose.note: Grose marks it as Oxford slang for an odd person; the meaning “test of questions” came later.

grose.head: ROW
grose.entry: ROW. A disturbance; a term used by the students at Cambridge.
grose.note: Still the British word for a noisy argument; the Dodger asks Oliver “What’s the row?”.

grose.head: SHAM
grose.entry: SHAM. A cheat, or trick. To cut a sham; to cheat or deceive. Shams; false sleeves to put on over a dirty shirt, or false sleeves with ruffles to put over a plain one. To sham Abram; to counterfeit sickness.
grose.note: Still used: something fake.

grose.head: SKIN FLINT
grose.entry: SKIN FLINT. An avaricious man or woman,
grose.note: Now one word: “skinflint” = a mean person.

grose.head: SLANG
grose.entry: SLANG. A fetter. Double slanged; double ironed. Now double slanged into the cells for a crop he is knocked down; he is double ironed in the condemned cells, and ordered to be hanged.
grose.note: Grose’s own definition of the word “slang”: the special language of thieves (cant).

grose.head: SNUG
grose.entry: SNUG. All's snug; all's quiet.
grose.note: Now means warm and comfortable.

grose.head: SPREE
grose.entry: SPREE. A frolic. Fun. A drinking bout. A party of pleasure.
grose.note: Still used: “a shopping spree”.

grose.head: TICK
grose.entry: TICK. To run o'tick; take up goods upon trust, to run in debt. Tick; a watch. SEE SESSIONS PAPERS.
grose.note: Still British: “on tick” = on credit.

grose.head: TOGS
grose.entry: TOGS. Clothes. The swell is rum-togged. The gentleman is handsomely dressed.
grose.note: Still informal British for clothes, especially for sport.

grose.head: TWADDLE
grose.entry: TWADDLE. Perplexity, confusion, or any thing else: a fashionable term that for a while succeeded that of BORE. See BORE.
grose.note: Still used: nonsense.

grose.head: WAG
grose.entry: WAG. An arch-frolicsome fellow.
grose.note: Old-fashioned: a joker.

grose.head: BEAK
grose.entry: BEAK. A justice of-peace, or magistrate. Also a judge or chairman who presides in court. I clapp'd my peepers full of tears, and so the old beak set me free; I began to weep, and the judge set me free.
grose.note: The Artful Dodger explains this word to Oliver: “a beak’s a madgst’rate”.

grose.head: FLASH
grose.entry: FLASH. Knowing. Understanding another's meaning. The swell was flash, so I could not draw his fogle. The gentleman saw what I was about, and therefore I could not pick his pocket of his silk handkerchief. To patter flash, to speak the slang language. See PATTER.
grose.note: The Dodger calls Oliver “my flash com-pan-i-on”. Now “flash” = showy.

grose.head: COVE
grose.entry: COVE. A man, a fellow, a rogue. The cove was bit; the rogue was outwitted. The cove has bit the cole; the rogue has got the money. CANT.
grose.note: The Dodger’s “my covey” is a pet form of this word.

grose.head: PRIG
grose.entry: PRIG. A thief, a cheat: also a conceited coxcomical fellow.
grose.note: Meaning has changed: today a “prig” is a self-righteous person.

grose.head: GIFT OF THE GAB
grose.entry: GIFT OF THE GAB. A facility of speech.
grose.note: Still used: “the gift of the gab” = talent for talking.

grose.head: CROCODILE'S TEARS
grose.entry: CROCODILE'S TEARS. The tears of a hypocrite. Crocodiles are fabulously reported to shed tears over their prey before they devour it.
grose.note: Still used: “crocodile tears” = false tears.

grose.head: BLARNEY
grose.entry: BLARNEY. He has licked the blarney stone; he deals in the wonderful, or tips us the traveller. The blarney stone is a triangular stone on the very top of an ancient castle of that name in the county of Cork in Ireland, extremely difficult of access; so that to have ascended to it, was considered as a proof of perseverance, courage, and agility, whereof many are supposed to claim the honour, who never atchieved the adventure: and to tip the blarney, is figuratively used telling a marvellous story, or falsity; and also sometimes to express flattery. Irish.
grose.note: Still used: flattering, charming talk (from the Blarney Stone in Ireland).

sayings.text: a word to the wise is enough

meaning.en: A wise person understands a short hint.

sayings.text: God helps them that help themselves

meaning.en: You must make an effort yourself.
meaning.ru: На Бога надейся, а сам не плошай.

sayings.text: Lost time is never found again
early to bed, and early to rise, makes a man healthy, wealthy, and wise

meaning.en: Good habits bring health and success.
meaning.ru: Кто рано встаёт, тому Бог подаёт.

sayings.text: The cat in gloves catches no mice

meaning.en: If you are too careful or polite, you get nothing done.
meaning.ru: Без труда не выловишь и рыбку из пруда.

sayings.text: little strokes fell great oaks

meaning.en: Many small efforts achieve great results. Also in Preston’s dictionary (No. 1549).

sayings.text: A small leak will sink a great ship

meaning.en: Small expenses or faults can ruin something big.

sayings.text: It is hard for an empty bag to stand upright

meaning.en: A poor or hungry person cannot easily be honest and strong.

sayings.text: Experience keeps a dear school, but fools will learn in no other

meaning.en: Fools learn only from painful experience. (Compare Preston No. 518.)
meaning.ru: Дураков учит только опыт — дорогая школа.

sayings.text: Far from the madding crowd

meaning.en: Far away from busy, noisy places. (Also the title of a Hardy novel.)

sayings.text: The paths of glory lead but to the grave

meaning.en: Fame cannot save anyone from death.
meaning.ru: Пути славы ведут лишь к могиле.

sayings.text: Stone walls do not a prison make

meaning.en: The mind can be free even when the body is not.

sayings.text: They also serve who only stand and waite

meaning.en: Patience and readiness are also a kind of service.
meaning.ru: Служит и тот, кто лишь стоит и ждёт.

sayings.text: The best-laid schemes o' mice an 'men

meaning.en: Even careful plans often go wrong.
meaning.ru: Лучшие планы мышей и людей часто рушатся.

sayings.text: Beauty is truth, truth beauty

meaning.en: Keats’s famous (and much debated) idea that beauty and truth are one.

sayings.text: If Winter comes, can Spring be far behind?

meaning.en: Hard times are followed by better ones.
meaning.ru: Если пришла зима, разве весна далеко?

sayings.text: To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield

meaning.en: Never give up searching and trying.
meaning.ru: Бороться и искать, найти и не сдаваться.

sayings.text: I am the master of my fate
sea-change
All’s right with the world
All art is quite useless.

meaning.en: Art does not need a practical purpose (Wilde’s provocation).

sayings.text: There is no such thing as a moral or an immoral book.  Books are well written, or badly written.  That is all.

meaning.en: Judge a book by its art, not its morals (Wilde’s view).
meaning.ru: Нет книг нравственных или безнравственных — есть написанные хорошо или плохо.
meaning.kz: Адамгершілікті не азғын кітап жоқ — жақсы не нашар жазылған кітап бар.

sayings.text: When critics disagree, the artist is in accord with himself.

meaning.en: Disagreement about a work shows it is new and alive.
meaning.ru: Когда критики расходятся, художник в согласии с собой.

phrases.line: It is the green-ey’d monster which doth mock
Nay, if thy wits run the wild-goose chase, I am done.
phrases.note: In Shakespeare’s time a wild-goose chase was a kind of horse race (Merriam-Webster).

phrases.line: My salad days,
phrases.note: Cleopatra meant “young and inexperienced”; today it often means “best years” (Merriam-Webster).

phrases.line: Might be the be-all and the end-all—here,
phrases.note: Now a noun phrase: “Money isn’t the be-all and end-all.”

phrases.line: But those that understood him smil’d at one another and shook their heads; but for mine own part, it was Greek to me.

meaning.en: I don’t understand it at all

phrases.note: Casca means it literally — Cicero spoke in Greek.

phrases.line: In my mind’s eye, Horatio.
phrases.note: Very common today. Horatio speaks of “the mind’s eye” earlier, in Scene I.

phrases.phrase: more in sorrow than in anger
phrases.line: A countenance more in sorrow than in anger.

meaning.ru: скорее с грустью, чем со злостью

phrases.phrase: something is rotten in the state of …
phrases.line: Something is rotten in the state of Denmark.
phrases.note: Often adapted: “Something is rotten in the state of …”.

phrases.line: I must be cruel, only to be kind:

meaning.en: hurting someone for their own good

phrases.note: “You have to be cruel to be kind.”

phrases.line: The lady protests too much, methinks.

meaning.en: by denying too strongly, someone shows it is true

phrases.note: Usually today: “The lady doth protest too much.”

phrases.line: [_Aside._] Though this be madness, yet there is method in’t.—

meaning.en: strange behaviour has a hidden purpose

phrases.phrase: to thine own self be true
phrases.line: This above all: to thine own self be true;

meaning.en: be honest about who you are

phrases.phrase: to wear your heart on your sleeve
phrases.line: But I will wear my heart upon my sleeve
phrases.note: Iago says it ironically — he hides everything.

phrases.line: But this denoted a foregone conclusion.

meaning.en: a result that is certain in advance

phrases.phrase: too much of a good thing
phrases.line: Why then, can one desire too much of a good thing?—Come, sister, you shall be the priest and marry us.—Give me your hand, Orlando.—What do you say, sister?

meaning.en: something pleasant that becomes too much

phrases.note: “You can have too much of a good thing.”

phrases.line: True is it that we have seen better days,

meaning.en: to be old or worn out

phrases.note: Used of things: “This sofa has seen better days.”

phrases.line: Are melted into air, into thin air:
But doth suffer a sea-change
How beauteous mankind is! O brave new world
phrases.note: Aldous Huxley took his novel’s title Brave New World from this line.

phrases.line: How cam’st thou in this pickle?
And I would call it fair play.
Should be without regard: what’s done is done.
At one fell swoop?
It is too full o’ th’ milk of human kindness
phrases.note: Lady Macbeth fears her husband has too much of it.

phrases.line: What, will the line stretch out to th’ crack of doom?

meaning.en: the end of the world; for ever

phrases.phrase: to eat someone out of house and home
phrases.line: He hath eaten me out of house and home.

meaning.en: to eat so much that someone becomes poor (humorous)

phrases.note: “My teenage son eats me out of house and home.”

phrases.line: The King’s a bawcock, and a heart of gold,
Straining upon the start. The game’s afoot!
phrases.note: Later used by Sherlock Holmes in Conan Doyle’s stories.

phrases.line: We few, we happy few, we band of brothers.

meaning.en: a close group who share danger

phrases.note: Used as the title of a famous TV series.

phrases.line: Besides, the King’s name is a tower of strength

meaning.en: a person who gives strong support

phrases.line: Off with his head! Now by Saint Paul I swear
phrases.note: Also the Queen of Hearts in Alice.

phrases.line: I’ll be sworn if thou be Launcelet, thou art mine own flesh and blood.
But love is blind, and lovers cannot see

meaning.en: people in love do not see faults

phrases.line: Give me your blessing, truth will come to light, murder cannot be hid long, a man’s son may, but in the end truth will out.
The devil can cite Scripture for his purpose.

meaning.en: bad people can quote good texts for their purposes

phrases.line: Cry havoc and let slip the dogs of war,
Beware the Ides of March.
_Et tu, Brute?_—Then fall, Caesar!

meaning.en: a cry at betrayal by a friend

phrases.phrase: uneasy lies the head that wears a crown
phrases.line: Uneasy lies the head that wears a crown.

phrases.phrase: such stuff as dreams are made on
phrases.line: Leave not a rack behind. We are such stuff

meaning.ru: из того же вещества, что и сны

phrases.phrase: (to be) more sinned against than sinning
phrases.line: More sinn’d against than sinning.

meaning.ru: больше грешны передо мной, чем я

phrases.line: Nothing will come of nothing: speak again.

meaning.en: you get nothing if you give nothing

phrases.line: Faith, and I’ll send him packing.
All the world’s a stage,
phrases.note: See the full speech in Shakespeare’s World.

prose.title: Oliver Twist — Chapter VIII: The Artful Dodger
prose.author: Charles Dickens
facts: Oliver Twist was published in monthly parts in 1837–39.
The Artful Dodger speaks London thieves’ cant: “beak”, “flash”, “grub”, “row” — words recorded in Grose’s Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811). See Voices: slang, cant & dialect.
prose.edition: Oliver Twist (Project Gutenberg eBook 730) — extract from Chapter VIII, “Oliver walks to London. He encounters on the road a strange sort of young gentleman”
prose.note: A hungry orphan meets a confident boy in a man’s coat who speaks the slang of the London streets. Read the dialogue aloud: Dickens spells the Dodger’s pronunciation (“sivin”, “madgst’rate”, “nothink”).

prose.title: Wuthering Heights — Chapter I
prose.author: Emily Brontë
facts: Published in 1847 under the pen-name Ellis Bell.
The novel is set on the Yorkshire moors; “wuthering” is a local word for stormy weather, as Lockwood explains in this chapter.
prose.edition: Wuthering Heights (Project Gutenberg eBook 768) — Chapter I, complete
prose.note: The narrator, Lockwood, visits his landlord Heathcliff at Wuthering Heights. Notice how Lockwood explains the local word “wuthering”, and how unwelcoming everyone at the house is.

prose.title: Three Men in a Boat — Chapter I
prose.author: Jerome K. Jerome
facts: Published in 1889; a comic account of a boating holiday on the River Thames.
prose.edition: Three Men in a Boat (To Say Nothing of the Dog) (Project Gutenberg eBook 308) — Chapter I, complete
prose.note: Three friends (and a dog) decide they are ill and need a holiday. The narrator reads a medical dictionary and finds he has every disease except one. English comic understatement at its best.

prose.title: The Wind in the Willows — Chapter I, “The River Bank” (opening)
prose.author: Kenneth Grahame
facts: Published in 1908.
fsrc: Encyclopaedia Britannica — The Wind in the Willows
prose.edition: The Wind in the Willows (Project Gutenberg eBook 289) — the opening of Chapter I
prose.note: Mole leaves his spring-cleaning and meets the Water Rat, who takes him on the river: “there is nothing … half so much worth doing as simply messing about in boats.”

prose.title: How the Whale Got His Throat
prose.author: Rudyard Kipling
facts: The first of the Just So Stories (1902), written for Kipling’s own children; each story ends with a poem.
prose.edition: Just So Stories (Project Gutenberg eBook 2781)
prose.note: A comic “why” story told to “O my Best Beloved”. Listen for Kipling’s word-play and rhymes inside the prose: “the plaice and the dace, and the skate and his mate”.

prose.title: Eveline
prose.author: James Joyce
facts: From Dubliners, a collection of short stories written 1904–07 and published in 1914.
prose.edition: Dubliners (Project Gutenberg eBook 2814)
prose.note: A young woman in Dublin must decide whether to leave home for a new life in Buenos Aires. A short story about one moment of choice — compare it with “Araby” from the same book.

prose.title: The Preface to The Picture of Dorian Gray
prose.author: Oscar Wilde
facts: The Preface first appeared in 1891, in answer to critics who had attacked the novel’s morality.
fsrc: Encyclopaedia Britannica — The Picture of Dorian Gray
prose.edition: The Picture of Dorian Gray (Project Gutenberg eBook 174) — the Preface, complete
prose.note: A chain of aphorisms (short, witty statements) about art. Wilde provokes: almost every sentence can be quoted alone. See also Sayings born in books.

prose.title: Through the Looking-Glass — Humpty Dumpty explains “Jabberwocky”
prose.author: Lewis Carroll
facts: Through the Looking-Glass was published at the end of 1871 (dated 1872).
Here Carroll explains his “portmanteau” words — two meanings packed into one word. The term is now used by linguists.
prose.edition: Through the Looking-Glass (Project Gutenberg eBook 12) — extract from Chapter VI
prose.note: A conversation about what words mean — and who decides. Read the poem “Jabberwocky” in Poetry first.

dodger.title: Oliver Twist — Chapter VIII: The Artful Dodger
body: He had been crouching on the step for some time: wondering at the great number of public-houses (every other house in Barnet was a tavern, large or small), gazing listlessly at the coaches as they passed through, and thinking how strange it seemed that they could do, with ease, in a few hours, what it had taken him a whole week of courage and determination beyond his years to accomplish: when he was roused by observing that a boy, who had passed him carelessly some minutes before, had returned, and was now surveying him most earnestly from the opposite side of the way.  He took little heed of this at first; but the boy remained in the same attitude of close observation so long, that Oliver raised his head, and returned his steady look.  Upon this, the boy crossed over; and walking close up to Oliver, said,
'Hullo, my covey!  What's the row?'

The boy who addressed this inquiry to the young wayfarer, was about his own age: but one of the queerest looking boys that Oliver had even seen.  He was a snub-nosed, flat-browed, common-faced boy enough; and as dirty a juvenile as one would wish to see; but he had about him all the airs and manners of a man.  He was short of his age: with rather bow-legs, and little, sharp, ugly eyes.  His hat was stuck on the top of his head so lightly, that it threatened to fall off every moment--and would have done so, very often, if the wearer had not had a knack of every now and then giving his head a sudden twitch, which brought it back to its old place again.  He wore a man's coat, which reached nearly to his heels.  He had turned the cuffs back, half-way up his arm, to get his hands out of the sleeves: apparently with the ultimate view of thrusting them into the pockets of his corduroy trousers; for there he kept them.  He was, altogether, as roystering and swaggering a young gentleman as ever stood four feet six, or something less, in the bluchers.
'Hullo, my covey!  What's the row?' said this strange young gentleman to Oliver.

'What mill!  Why, _the_ mill--the mill as takes up so little room that it'll work inside a Stone Jug; and always goes better when the wind's low with people, than when it's high; acos then they can't get workmen. But come,' said the young gentleman; 'you want grub, and you shall have it.  I'm at low-water-mark myself--only one bob and a magpie; but, as far as it goes, I'll fork out and stump.  Up with you on your pins. There!  Now then! 'Morrice!'

'Don't fret your eyelids on that score,' said the young gentleman. 'I've got to be in London to-night; and I know a 'spectable old gentleman as lives there, wot'll give you lodgings for nothink, and never ask for the change--that is, if any genelman he knows interduces you. And don't he know me?  Oh, no! Not in the least!  By no means. Certainly not!'

wuthering1.title: Wuthering Heights — Chapter I
body: 1801.--I have just returned from a visit to my landlord--the solitary neighbour that I shall be troubled with.  This is certainly a beautiful country!  In all England, I do not believe that I could have fixed on a situation so completely removed from the stir of society.  A perfect misanthropist's heaven: and Mr. Heathcliff and I are such a suitable pair to divide the desolation between us.  A capital fellow!  He little imagined how my heart warmed towards him when I beheld his black eyes withdraw so suspiciously under their brows, as I rode up, and when his fingers sheltered themselves, with a jealous resolution, still further in his waistcoat, as I announced my name.
'Mr. Heathcliff?' I said.
A nod was the answer.

'Mr. Lockwood, your new tenant, sir.  I do myself the honour of calling as soon as possible after my arrival, to express the hope that I have not inconvenienced you by my perseverance in soliciting the occupation of Thrushcross Grange: I heard yesterday you had had some thoughts--'

threemen1.title: Three Men in a Boat — Chapter I
body: There were four of us—George, and William Samuel Harris, and myself, and Montmorency.  We were sitting in my room, smoking, and talking about how bad we were—bad from a medical point of view I mean, of course.

We were all feeling seedy, and we were getting quite nervous about it. Harris said he felt such extraordinary fits of giddiness come over him at times, that he hardly knew what he was doing; and then George said that _he_ had fits of giddiness too, and hardly knew what _he_ was doing. With me, it was my liver that was out of order.  I knew it was my liver that was out of order, because I had just been reading a patent liver-pill circular, in which were detailed the various symptoms by which a man could tell when his liver was out of order.  I had them all.

It is a most extraordinary thing, but I never read a patent medicine advertisement without being impelled to the conclusion that I am suffering from the particular disease therein dealt with in its most virulent form.  The diagnosis seems in every case to correspond exactly with all the sensations that I have ever felt.

[Picture: Man reading book] I remember going to the British Museum one day to read up the treatment for some slight ailment of which I had a touch—hay fever, I fancy it was.  I got down the book, and read all I came to read; and then, in an unthinking moment, I idly turned the leaves, and began to indolently study diseases, generally.  I forget which was the first distemper I plunged into—some fearful, devastating scourge, I know—and, before I had glanced half down the list of “premonitory symptoms,” it was borne in upon me that I had fairly got it.

willows1.title: The Wind in the Willows — Chapter I, “The River Bank” (opening)
body: The Mole had been working very hard all the morning, spring-cleaning his little home. First with brooms, then with dusters; then on ladders and steps and chairs, with a brush and a pail of whitewash; till he had dust in his throat and eyes, and splashes of whitewash all over his black fur, and an aching back and weary arms. Spring was moving in the air above and in the earth below and around him, penetrating even his dark and lowly little house with its spirit of divine discontent and longing. It was small wonder, then, that he suddenly flung down his brush on the floor, said ‘Bother!’ and ‘O blow!’ and also ‘Hang spring-cleaning!’ and bolted out of the house without even waiting to put on his coat. Something up above was calling him imperiously, and he made for the steep little tunnel which answered in his case to the gravelled carriage-drive owned by animals whose residences are nearer to the sun and air. So he scraped and scratched and scrabbled and scrooged and then he scrooged again and scrabbled and scratched and scraped, working busily with his little paws and muttering to himself, ‘Up we go! Up we go!’ till at last, pop! his snout came out into the sunlight, and he found himself rolling in the warm grass of a great meadow.

‘This is fine!’ he said to himself. ‘This is better than whitewashing!’ The sunshine struck hot on his fur, soft breezes caressed his heated brow, and after the seclusion of the cellarage he had lived in so long the carol of happy birds fell on his dulled hearing almost like a shout. Jumping off all his four legs at once, in the joy of living and the delight of spring without its cleaning, he pursued his way across the meadow till he reached the hedge on the further side.

‘Hold up!’ said an elderly rabbit at the gap. ‘Sixpence for the privilege of passing by the private road!’ He was bowled over in an instant by the impatient and contemptuous Mole, who trotted along the side of the hedge chaffing the other rabbits as they peeped hurriedly from their holes to see what the row was about. ‘Onion-sauce! Onion-sauce!’ he remarked jeeringly, and was gone before they could think of a thoroughly satisfactory reply. Then they all started grumbling at each other. ‘How STUPID you are! Why didn’t you tell him----’ ‘Well, why didn’t YOU say----’ ‘You might have reminded him----’ and so on, in the usual way; but, of course, it was then much too late, as is always the case.

It all seemed too good to be true. Hither and thither through the meadows he rambled busily, along the hedgerows, across the copses, finding everywhere birds building, flowers budding, leaves thrusting--everything happy, and progressive, and occupied. And instead of having an uneasy conscience pricking him and whispering ‘whitewash!’ he somehow could only feel how jolly it was to be the only idle dog among all these busy citizens. After all, the best part of a holiday is perhaps not so much to be resting yourself, as to see all the other fellows busy working.

‘Nice? It’s the ONLY thing,’ said the Water Rat solemnly, as he leant forward for his stroke. ‘Believe me, my young friend, there is NOTHING--absolute nothing--half so much worth doing as simply messing about in boats. Simply messing,’ he went on dreamily: ‘messing--about--in--boats; messing----’

whale.title: How the Whale Got His Throat
body: IN the sea, once upon a time, O my Best Beloved, there was a Whale, and he ate fishes. He ate the starfish and the garfish, and the crab and the dab, and the plaice and the dace, and the skate and his mate, and the mackereel and the pickereel, and the really truly twirly-whirly eel. All the fishes he could find in all the sea he ate with his mouth--so! Till at last there was only one small fish left in all the sea, and he was a small ‘Stute Fish, and he swam a little behind the Whale’s right ear, so as to be out of harm’s way. Then the Whale stood up on his tail and said, ‘I’m hungry.’ And the small ‘Stute Fish said in a small ‘stute voice, ‘Noble and generous Cetacean, have you ever tasted Man?’
‘No,’ said the Whale. ‘What is it like?’
‘Nice,’ said the small ‘Stute Fish. ‘Nice but nubbly.’
‘Then fetch me some,’ said the Whale, and he made the sea froth up with his tail.

eveline.title: Eveline
body: She sat at the window watching the evening invade the avenue. Her head was leaned against the window curtains and in her nostrils was the odour of dusty cretonne. She was tired.

Few people passed. The man out of the last house passed on his way home; she heard his footsteps clacking along the concrete pavement and afterwards crunching on the cinder path before the new red houses. One time there used to be a field there in which they used to play every evening with other people’s children. Then a man from Belfast bought the field and built houses in it—not like their little brown houses but bright brick houses with shining roofs. The children of the avenue used to play together in that field—the Devines, the Waters, the Dunns, little Keogh the cripple, she and her brothers and sisters. Ernest, however, never played: he was too grown up. Her father used often to hunt them in out of the field with his blackthorn stick; but usually little Keogh used to keep nix and call out when he saw her father coming. Still they seemed to have been rather happy then. Her father was not so bad then; and besides, her mother was alive. That was a long time ago; she and her brothers and sisters were all grown up; her mother was dead. Tizzie Dunn was dead, too, and the Waters had gone back to England. Everything changes. Now she was going to go away like the others, to leave her home.

Home! She looked round the room, reviewing all its familiar objects which she had dusted once a week for so many years, wondering where on earth all the dust came from. Perhaps she would never see again those familiar objects from which she had never dreamed of being divided. And yet during all those years she had never found out the name of the priest whose yellowing photograph hung on the wall above the broken harmonium beside the coloured print of the promises made to Blessed Margaret Mary Alacoque. He had been a school friend of her father. Whenever he showed the photograph to a visitor her father used to pass it with a casual word:
“He is in Melbourne now.”

dorian-preface.title: The Preface to The Picture of Dorian Gray
body: The artist is the creator of beautiful things.  To reveal art and conceal the artist is art's aim.  The critic is he who can translate into another manner or a new material his impression of beautiful things.
The highest as the lowest form of criticism is a mode of autobiography. Those who find ugly meanings in beautiful things are corrupt without being charming.  This is a fault.
Those who find beautiful meanings in beautiful things are the cultivated.  For these there is hope.  They are the elect to whom beautiful things mean only beauty.
There is no such thing as a moral or an immoral book.  Books are well written, or badly written.  That is all.

humpty.title: Through the Looking-Glass — Humpty Dumpty explains “Jabberwocky”
body: ‘I don’t know what you mean by “glory,”’ Alice said.
Humpty Dumpty smiled contemptuously. ‘Of course you don’t--till I tell you. I meant “there’s a nice knock-down argument for you!”’
‘But “glory” doesn’t mean “a nice knock-down argument,”’ Alice objected.
‘When _I_ use a word,’ Humpty Dumpty said in rather a scornful tone, ‘it means just what I choose it to mean--neither more nor less.’

marlowe.name: Christopher Marlowe
marlowe.bio: Playwright and poet, born the same year as Shakespeare. Author of Doctor Faustus (see Drama).

raleigh.name: Sir Walter Raleigh
raleigh.bio: Courtier, explorer and poet at the court of Elizabeth I.

jonson.name: Ben Jonson
jonson.bio: Playwright and poet, Shakespeare’s friend and rival. He wrote the poem in the First Folio calling Shakespeare “not of an age, but for all time”.

herbert.name: George Herbert
herbert.bio: Priest and poet. His religious poems were published after his death in The Temple (1633).

milton.name: John Milton
milton.bio: Poet of Paradise Lost. He was blind for the last twenty years of his life and dictated his poems.

lovelace.name: Richard Lovelace
lovelace.bio: Royalist soldier and poet, imprisoned during the English Civil War.

gray.name: Thomas Gray
gray.bio: Scholar and poet at Cambridge. He published very little; his Elegy made him famous.

coleridge.name: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
coleridge.bio: Romantic poet and critic, Wordsworth’s friend and co-author of Lyrical Ballads (1798).

poe.name: Edgar Allan Poe
poe.bio: American poet and short-story writer, master of mystery and horror.

whitman.name: Walt Whitman
whitman.bio: American poet of Leaves of Grass, a pioneer of free verse.

browning.name: Robert Browning
browning.bio: Victorian poet, master of the dramatic monologue. Husband of Elizabeth Barrett Browning.

ebb.name: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
ebb.bio: One of the most famous poets of her time. She married Robert Browning in 1846 and lived in Italy.

emilybronte.name: Emily Brontë
emilybronte.bio: Poet and novelist, author of Wuthering Heights (1847). She published under the name Ellis Bell.

arnold.name: Matthew Arnold
arnold.bio: Victorian poet, critic and school inspector.

hopkins.name: Gerard Manley Hopkins
hopkins.bio: Jesuit priest and poet. His poems, with their new “sprung rhythm”, were published only in 1918.

henley.name: William Ernest Henley
henley.bio: Poet, editor and critic. Friend of Robert Louis Stevenson.

kipling.name: Rudyard Kipling
kipling.bio: Poet and story-writer, Nobel Prize in Literature 1907. His views on empire are much criticised today.

hardy.name: Thomas Hardy
hardy.bio: Novelist (Far from the Madding Crowd, Tess) who turned to poetry later in life.

housman.name: A. E. Housman
housman.bio: Classical scholar and poet of A Shropshire Lad (1896).

brooke.name: Rupert Brooke
brooke.bio: Poet who died on active service in 1915, aged 27.

carroll.name: Lewis Carroll
carroll.bio: Pen-name of Charles Dodgson, Oxford mathematician and author of the Alice books.

words.produce: Find three more “spoken spellings” in the Dodger extract.

anchor.needle: brevity is the soul of wit

words.note: Polonius says “brevity is the soul of wit” — and then talks for a long time. Old sense survives in “at your wits’ end”, “quick-witted”.
words.produce: When were you “at your wits’ end”?

anchor.needle: The quality of mercy is not strain’d

words.note: Portia: mercy cannot be forced out of anyone — it falls freely like rain.
words.fig: Mercy is compared to gentle rain, which no one can force.
words.produce: Write a sentence with “strained relations” (modern meaning).
words.now: tense, not relaxed; (of a muscle) injured

words.note: About climate and character: “a temperate climate”, “temperate language”.
words.produce: Is your city’s climate temperate? Explain.

meaning.en: too much of something (until you feel sick of it)

words.note: Orsino wants so much music that his love will die of too much.
words.produce: Describe a surfeit of something modern (news, messages…).

anchor.needle: Summer’s lease hath all too short a date

meaning.en: a limited time you are allowed to have something

words.note: Summer “rents” its days, and the contract ends too soon (date = end date).
words.fig: Summer is a tenant whose rental period is short.
words.produce: Use “a new lease of life” in a sentence.

words.word: a consummation devoutly to be wished

meaning.en: an end that one should truly hope for

words.note: Today often humorous: about something very desirable.
words.produce: Name something that would be “a consummation devoutly to be wished” for you.

meaning.en: loud anger or noise that means nothing

words.note: Faulkner used it as a novel title (1929). Today about empty protests or speeches.
words.produce: Describe a debate that was “all sound and fury”.

anchor.needle: Ambition should be made of sterner stuff

words.note: Common today: “She is made of sterner stuff.”
words.produce: Describe someone made of sterner stuff.

anchor.needle: the ancient grudge I bear him

meaning.en: keep feeling anger about an old wrong

words.note: Collocation: bear / hold a grudge (against someone).
words.fig: Shylock will “feed fat” his grudge — as if it were an animal.
words.produce: Do you ever bear a grudge? Explain.

anchor.needle: How transitory we be all day

words.note: Synonyms: transient, fleeting. Note the old grammar “we be” = we are.
words.produce: Name three transitory things that people value too much.

anchor.needle: For though I mourn it availeth nought

words.note: Nought = nothing. Today: “to no avail” = without success.
words.produce: Use “to no avail” in a sentence.

meaning.en: black magic; talking with the dead

words.note: Greek nekros (dead) + manteia (prophecy).
words.produce: Which other words do you know with “necro-” or “-mancy”?

anchor.needle: the greater the coxcomb, always the more the scandal

words.note: From the jester’s cap shaped like a cock’s comb.
words.produce: Describe a modern “coxcomb” in two sentences.

meaning.en: inventing an imaginary friend as an excuse to escape duties

words.note: Wilde’s invented word from Algernon’s imaginary invalid friend Bunbury.
words.produce: Describe a modern way of “Bunburying”.

words.note: Algernon’s joke: an idea that is “exploded” is no longer believed. Also: “an exploded theory”.
words.fig: Lady Bracknell hears it literally — as if Bunbury blew up.
words.produce: Name an “exploded” myth about learning languages.

anchor.needle: may be regarded as a misfortune

words.note: Lady Bracknell: losing one parent is a misfortune; losing both “looks like carelessness”. The joke is her cold logic.
words.produce: Explain why Lady Bracknell’s line is funny.

meaning.en: spending far too much without thinking

words.note: Strong collocation: reckless + spending/driving/behaviour.
words.produce: Describe an act of reckless extravagance.

meaning.en: a poor, dirty child who lives in the streets (insulting)

words.note: Higgins insults Eliza; “draggletailed” = with a dirty, wet skirt.
words.produce: How does Higgins speak about Eliza? Find two insulting words.

words.note: In 1914 this word on stage caused a sensation. It shows how register changes: now mild British slang, then shocking.
words.produce: Why did the audience gasp in 1914 but not today?

anchor.needle: I’m only a squashed cabbage leaf

meaning.en: a worthless thing (Eliza repeats Higgins’s insult)

words.note: Eliza throws Higgins’s own words back at him.
words.fig: Eliza is not a leaf — she is treated like rubbish.
words.produce: Turn an insult into a strong reply.

words.note: Higgins’s cruel simile; bilious = feeling sick.
words.fig: Eliza’s sounds are compared to a sick bird.
words.produce: Write a funny (not cruel) simile for a sound.

meaning.en: cry loudly for the dead (Irish tradition)

words.note: From Irish caoineadh. Different from the adjective keen (eager).
words.produce: Does your culture have a tradition like keening? Describe it.

words.note: Shelley means ancient Egypt, not old furniture.
words.produce: Describe an antique object you have seen.

meaning.en: copied, imitated (and perhaps also laughed at)

words.note: A double meaning: the sculptor copied the king’s passions — and made fun of them.
words.produce: Explain the two meanings of “mocked” in this line.

words.note: Lewis Carroll invented it (chuckle + snort). It is now in every dictionary.
words.produce: Use “chortle” in a sentence.

meaning.en: move in a noisy, clumsy, happy way

words.note: Another Carroll invention (gallop + triumph) that entered English.
words.produce: Describe a dog galumphing across a field.

anchor.needle: Old Marley was as dead as a door-nail

meaning.ru: мёртвый, как гвоздь в двери (совершенно мёртвый)

words.note: Dickens jokes that he does not know what is especially dead about a door-nail. The phrase is much older (14th century).
words.fig: Not about real nails: the meaning is “totally”.
words.produce: Use “as dead as a doornail” about a phone or a plan.

words.note: Scrooge’s famous “Bah! Humbug!”. In Britain a humbug is also a striped mint sweet.
words.produce: What would Scrooge call “humbug” today?

meaning.en: wanting other people’s money or things very much

words.note: Dickens piles up seven adjectives: squeezing, wrenching, grasping, scraping, clutching, covetous, old.
words.produce: Describe a character with three -ing adjectives, like Dickens.

anchor.needle: he was a tight-fisted hand at the grind-stone

words.note: A hand at the grindstone = always working hard (to make money).
words.fig: His fist is closed tight around his money.
words.produce: Describe a tight-fisted person you have read about.

meaning.en: completely alone and closed to others

words.note: An oyster is shut in its shell.
words.fig: Scrooge is closed like an oyster’s shell.
words.produce: Write your own simile for a lonely person.

anchor.needle: It is a truth universally acknowledged

words.note: The most famous first line in English fiction — and it is ironic: the mothers, not the rich men, believe it.
words.produce: Write an ironic opening: “It is a truth universally acknowledged that…”

anchor.needle: must be in want of a wife

words.note: Old meaning of want = lack (as in Shakespeare).
words.produce: Use “in want of” in a formal sentence.

anchor.needle: I have a high respect for your nerves

meaning.en: Mrs Bennet’s “nerves”: a nervous, easily upset state she often complains of

words.note: Mr Bennet is sarcastic: he has heard about her nerves for twenty years.
words.produce: Use “get on someone’s nerves” in a sentence.
words.now: courage; or anxiety before an event

words.note: Jane reads about the Arctic and feels its loneliness.
words.produce: Describe a forlorn region you have seen in a film.

words.note: The tale keeps the Suffolk voice of its teller: “they’ll come again” = they will become soft.
words.produce: Rewrite the mother’s line in standard English.

words.word: some books are to be tasted

anchor.needle: Some books are to be tasted, others to be swallowed, and some few to be chewed and digested

meaning.en: read some books in parts, some quickly, and a few slowly and carefully
meaning.ru: одни книги надо пробовать, другие — глотать, а немногие — разжёвывать и переваривать
meaning.kz: кейбір кітапты дәмін тату, кейбірін жұту, кейбірін шайнап қорыту керек

words.note: Bacon explains his own metaphor right after it.
words.fig: Reading = eating.
words.produce: Name one book to taste, one to swallow and one to chew.

words.note: Bacon’s triple pattern: reading → full, conference (talk) → ready, writing → exact.
words.produce: Write a triple sentence in Bacon’s style about learning English.

anchor.needle: many weened to have been king

words.note: Survives only in the adjective overweening (= too proud).
words.produce: Use “overweening ambition” in a sentence.

anchor.needle: Time and tide tarry for no man

words.note: Tide here first meant “time, season” (compare Christmastide). The modern proverb says “wait for no man”.
words.produce: Rewrite the proverb in modern English.

words.word: count your chickens before they are hatched

anchor.needle: Count not your chickens before they are hatched

meaning.en: expect success before it has happened

words.note: Old negative imperative: “Count not” = Don’t count.
words.fig: Not real chickens: plans and hopes.
words.produce: Describe a time someone counted their chickens too early.

words.word: every cloud has a silver lining

anchor.needle: Every cloud hath a silver lining

meaning.en: something good comes from every bad situation

words.note: Hath = has. The image goes back to Milton’s Comus (1634).
words.fig: A dark cloud shines at its edge.
words.produce: Find the silver lining in a bad day you had.

anchor.needle: Do not holloa till you are out of the wood

words.note: Today: “Don’t count your chickens…” has a similar meaning; the American form is “out of the woods”.
words.fig: The wood = danger; leaving it = safety.
words.produce: When are you really “out of the woods”?

meaning.en: a rule or principle for behaviour

words.note: Example (what you do) vs precept (what you say).
words.produce: Who taught you by example, not by precept?
